newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil announces new land tax to speed up reform.
newsitem.headline: Brazil announces new land tax to speed up reform.

text.p: Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso announced on Tuesday a new rural land tax to speed up reform of Brazil's unequal land distribution, one of the country's most serious problems.
The new ITR rural land tax was included in a decree which has to be approved by Congress and will take effect as soon as it is published in the government's official gazette.
The ITR tax is mainly aimed at landowners of unproductive properties, who will have to pay an annual tax of up to 20 percent on the value of their land.

"The tax collection will be rigorous in the case of large unproductive landholdings. And it will put a stop to tax evasion which occurs in 88 percent (of these type of landholdings)," Cardoso said in a weekly radio broadcast hours before he announced the measure.
"By sending the ITR proposal to Congress we will be turning the page on 500 years of history of injustice...which resulted in one of the worst concentrations of land in the world," Cardoso added.
The new tax will range from 0.05 percent on productive properties of up to 50 hectares to 20 percent on landholdings of up to 5,000 hectares which make use of less than 30 percent of their land.
Land considered unproductive and whose owners do not pay the new tax can be confiscated by the state after five years and included in the agrarian reform program.
Eighty percent of Brazil's farm land belongs to 10 percent of the population, with 49,000 landowners each holding an average 3,347 hectares, according to the Catholic Church's land commission (CPT).

The CPT blames this situation for the increasing number of conflicts between landless peasants and landowners, which has left 90 people dead since January 1995, including those killed during police operations to remove squatters.
The landless peasant movement (MST), which is pursuing an active campaign to recover land for an estimated 4.8 million landless families, gave a lukewarm welcome to the government's proposal.

"We sympathize with this measure, but (the tax increase) is not the main problem (of agriculture in Brazil)," MST national coordinator Francisco Dalchiavon told Reuters. "The important issue is the government's decision to collect the tax and to commit itself to carry out agrarian reform."
Cardoso said the new tax came in response to "an old demand by workers, farmers, landowners, unions and employers and employee associations", as well as churches, including the Catholic Church.
The Minister for Agrarian Reform, Raul Jungman, said the receipts from the ITR tax would increase to $1.5 billion in the next two years from $300 million in 1996.
"And all this money will go directly towards agrarian reform," Jungman said.
